narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other, aligned so that one star periodically blocks light from the other as seen from Earth. TESS observes hundreds of thousands of stars, and our pipeline searches their light curves for the telltale dips that signal eclipses. We measure orbital period and eclipse depths, then cross-check candidates against six major variable-star catalogs to flag known objects. Candidates that pass statistical vetting and appear novel go through a pixel-level contamination check - a fully automated scan to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself, not a nearby interloper. A machine-learning model trained on over 1700 labeled examples provides a second opinion on each candidate, outperforming our baseline approach. We have confirmed 178 candidates so far by examining about 1.4% of TESS's full sky coverage. Each candidate listing includes its measured properties and any relevant caveats so researchers can evaluate it for their own purposes.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting around their common center of mass. From Earth's perspective, their orbital plane is tilted so that one star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. These eclipses show up as regular dips in the star's brightness. By analyzing the timing and depth of these dips, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, separation, and orbital period.

faqs.question: What do you mean by 'candidate' versus 'confirmed'?
faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is any star whose light curve shows a pattern consistent with eclipsing. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that has passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level contamination check, meaning the eclipse signal comes from the target star and not from a nearby star or artifact. 'Confirmed' is this pipeline's own internal term for that automated checkpoint. It does not mean the candidate has been verified by independent observation, spectroscopy, or professional follow-up.

faqs.question: What is the machine-learning screening score?
faqs.answer: We trained a machine-learning model (histogram gradient boosting) on 1738 labeled examples to score each candidate. It outperforms our rule-based baseline approach. However, the ML score is a second opinion only - it does not currently gate or filter which candidates advance through the pipeline. All candidates that pass statistical vetting and novelty checking proceed to the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score.

faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?
faqs.answer: After a candidate passes initial statistical vetting, an automated pixel-level contamination check scans whether the eclipse signal is centered on the target star or scattered across nearby pixels that might indicate a blended neighbor. This is a fully automated procedure, not a manual review. Candidates that pass this check are marked as confirmed and listed on our site.

faqs.question: What happens if the orbital period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: TESS observes stars continuously, but eclipses in a light curve can sometimes fold into the data in multiple ways, creating ambiguous periods. To test for this, we compare the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If they differ significantly, it may signal a period alias rather than a true period. This check helps flag candidates that warrant caution.

faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate is listed with its measured orbital period and eclipse depths, derived from the TESS light curve. You can download TESS data for the target star and examine the light curve yourself to see if the eclipses match the published values. Each candidate page also includes any relevant caveats noted during vetting.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the endpoint of this automated pipeline. We do not perform spectroscopic follow-up, coordinate observations, add candidates to official catalogs, or track their use by other researchers. Our role is to flag promising candidates and measure their light-curve properties. What happens next - observations, spectroscopy, or inclusion in other studies - is up to the broader astronomical community.
